papers.title_in_file: Solving Large-Scale QUBO with Transferred Parameters from Multilevel QAOA of low depth
papers.version_note: arXiv:2505.11464v1, 16 May 2025. The text layer holds the paper once. Table I and Figures 1 to 4 are partly lost or garbled, so table values and plot contents are not entered.
papers.what_it_is: A multilevel QAOA method for large QUBO and MAXCUT instances that transfers p = 1 parameters from the coarsest level to finer levels and combines Quantum Relax & Round with a genetic algorithm, tested by classical simulation on graphs of 3437 to 14000 nodes.

existing.note: The Discussion lists three open directions. The stored value holds a) and b) but not c), the improvement of the coarsening and refinement schemes. The Discussion is Section VI, not a Conclusion section.
existing.value: The authors list as open: proving the parameter transfer analytically for p = 1 QAOA+QRR within the multilevel setup for toy problems; investigating the performance of their method for higher circuit depth; and devising further improvements of the coarsening and refinement schemes, for example via changing the topology and/or dimension of the embedding.
quotes: proving the parameter transfer analytically for p = 1 QAOA+QRR within the multilevel setup for toy problems
investigating the performance of our method for higher circuit depth
devising further improvements of the coarsening and refinement schemes, for example via changing the topology and/or dimension of the embedding
existing.certainty_reason: The authors state these as open directions in Section VI (Discussion).

quotes: we employ QRR specifically for the p = 1 QAOA regime, where analytic expressions for spin correlations are available [9]
collecting extensive samples for largescale problems remains infeasible

existing.reader_inference: The stored anchor names Section III; in this version the passage is in Section II-C. The value is right.

existing.note: The passage is in the opening of Section IV (Methods), not Section II. The same sentence adds that the transfer reduces the need for parameter optimization at all levels except the coarsest. The paper's landscape-similarity analysis (Section V-A) is the numerical support.
quotes: we numerically observe that for p = 1 circuits, the optimal parameters are approximately transferred between the circuits at different levels of the hierarchy
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical observation from one study.
existing.reader_inference: The support in the text is a landscape-overlap measure shown for one example graph (Fig. 3) and the solver comparison on G1. The paper does not report running the solver with transfer against one without.

existing.note: The statement is right. Two limits sit in the paper around it. The comparison is of the two multilevel columns of Table I, where each multilevel solution warm-starts a Burer-Monteiro run. Section V also states that the p = 1 multilevel solver alone is not of sufficient quality to compete with state-of-the-art classical solvers. The depth claim is an expectation, not a result.
existing.anchor: Section V-B, p.6, after Table I

We anticipate that increasing the QAOA depth would further enhance solution quality.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, simulated classically. The depth statement is an anticipation.
existing.reader_inference: Counting the 17 graph rows of Table I (higher is better), the QAOA+BURER02 column is higher in 10 rows, the ML BURER02 column is higher in 6 rows and the two are equal in 1 row. This count is the reader's, from the table, and the table is not quoted.

assertions.value: The authors propose a hybrid multilevel algorithm with QAOA parameterization throughout the multilevel hierarchy, reinforced with genetic algorithms, which they describe as a low-depth QAOA solver.
quotes: we propose a fast hybrid multilevel algorithm with QAOA parameterization throughout the multilevel hierarchy and its reinforcement with genetic algorithms
which results in a high-quality, low-depth QAOA solver
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states what the authors built.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract calls the solver high-quality. Section V states that the p = 1 multilevel solver alone does not compete with state-of-the-art classical solvers, so that wording is not a measured result.

assertions.value: The authors state that existing multilevel QAOA implementations can be restrictive in two respects: the variational parameters are not inherited throughout uncoarsening, and QAOA is not hybridized with fast classical approaches at all levels of coarseness.
quotes: existing multilevel QAOA implementations can be restrictive in two key respects: (1) the variational parameters are not inherited throughout uncoarsening
(2) QAOA is not hybridized with fast classical approaches to fully exploit joint potential at all levels of coarseness
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' characterization of prior work, with no test in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the relaxation-based coarsening preserves essential QUBO information, and that they support this claim with numerical evidence.
quotes: This is because the relaxation-based coarsening preserves essential QUBO information—a claim we support with numerical evidence.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim. The only numerical support in the text is the landscape-overlap measure for one example and the G1 solver comparison.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not test the coarsening against a different coarsening on the same instances, apart from the one illustrated example in Fig. 1.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Dunning et al., that an n-variable QUBO problem can be transformed to an n+1-node MAXCUT problem up to a multiplicative factor, and that MAXCUT is equivalent to an Ising model without external fields, so QAOA solves a QUBO problem as a MAXCUT problem identified with a spin Ising Hamiltonian.
quotes: Given n−variable QUBO problem, it can be transformed to
n+1-node MAXCUT problem up to a multiplicative factor by
it as n+1-node MAXCUT and identify it with n+1-spin Ising
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to reference [11].

assertions.value: The authors describe Quantum Relax & Round, proposed in reference [10], as approximating the two-point correlations of spins in the QAOA state, eigendecomposing the correlation matrix Z, sign-rounding the resulting eigenvectors and evaluating the rounded vectors as potential solutions.
quotes: [10] proposed an efficient Quantum Relax & Round (QRR) algorithm inspired by classical relax & round strategies
QRR performs an eigendecomposition of Z, sign-rounds the resulting eigenvectors, and evaluates these rounded vectors as potential solutions
assertions.certainty_reason: A method the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that they adopt the canonical, simplest V-cycle scheme, explicitly to observe the effects of p = 1 QAOA in a controlled setting and to minimize additional advantages from advanced classical preprocessing.
quotes: we adopt the canonical, simplest V-cycle scheme, explicitly to observe the effects of p = 1 QAOA in a controlled setting, and to minimize additional advantages from advanced classical preprocessing
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own design choice in Section II-D.

assertions.value: The authors state that coarsening starts by randomly embedding the nodes of the graph onto the surface of a 3-dimensional sphere, followed by a heuristic node-wise iterative correction that maximizes the weighted distance between each node and its neighbors, with a closed-form solution for each point from a Lagrange-multiplier solution, iterated until convergence.
quotes: the coarsening starts with randomly embedding the nodes of graph Gl onto a surface of a 3−dimensional sphere
a heuristic node-wise iterative correction is applied to maximize the weighted distance between each node and its neighbors
achieves a closed-form solution for each point (i.e., node) i ∈ Vl through the Lagrange-multiplier solution of Equation 2
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors describe their own method in Section IV-A.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer has the sentence "while bounding neighbors connected by positive weight" after "separating nodes from their neighbors connected by positive weight". The second probably means negative weight, but this is the reader's reading, not the text.

assertions.value: The authors define Threshold Pairwise Merging: nodes i and j are paired only if dij ≤ max{∆1d¯, ∆2 min d} and wij ≤ 0, where d is the matrix of pairwise distances and d¯ (min d) denotes the average (minimum) distance, with the threshold hyperparameters ∆1, ∆2 setting how strictly nodes are merged.
quotes: we start pairing nodes only if for two nodes i and j, we have dij ≤ max{∆1d¯, ∆2 min d}
and wij ≤ 0, where d is the matrix of pairwise distances,
d¯ (min d) denotes the average (minimum) distance
threshold hyperparameters ∆1, ∆2, which determine how strictly we want to merge the nodes
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the merging rule in Section IV-A.

assertions.value: The authors state that the earlier Logarithmic Pairwise Merging can merge nodes with relatively high distances and converge to lower quality coarsened representations, that Threshold Pairwise Merging may result in more levels at the gain of improved quality, and that in the caption example the second strategy introduces one more level but captures the original graph cost correctly.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-A and Fig. 1 caption, p.3-4
quotes: can sometimes lead to merging nodes with relatively high
This condition may result in more levels, at the gain of improved quality.
The second strategy introduces one more level but captures the original graph cost correctly.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim supported by one small illustrative example. No measurement of the two merging rules on benchmark graphs is reported.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no ablation of Threshold against Logarithmic Pairwise Merging on the Gset or SuiteSparse graphs.

assertions.value: The authors state that they perform large-scale simulations based on the scalable analytical form of p = 1 QAOA, and that QAOA expectation values are simulated classically at a cost of order n squared (printed "O(n2)") for p = 1, so no quantum hardware run is reported.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-B and Section V, p.4
quotes: we perform large-scale simulations based on the scalable analytical form of p = 1 QAOA [9]
(note that for higher p, QAOA is generally hard to simulate)
in our experiments, QAOA expectation values are simulated classically, which has O(n2) complexity for p = 1
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state how the experiments were run in Sections IV-B and V.
assertions.reader_inference: The clause "so no quantum hardware run is reported" is the reader's reading of the text: every result uses classically simulated expectation values.

assertions.value: The authors state that at the coarsest level a simple grid optimizer identifies suitable parameter sets and stores the resulting correlation matrices, Quantum Relax & Round is applied to each matrix, and the best s candidates across all parameter sets form the initial population of a genetic algorithm that outputs the best solution at the coarsest level.
quotes: At the coarsest level, a simple grid optimizer identifies suitable parameter sets
We then perform Quantum Relax & Round to each matrix Z to produce the top candidate solutions for each set of parameters.
The best s of those candidates (across all parameter sets) are then used as an initial population of the genetic algorithm (GA)
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors describe their own procedure in Section IV-B.
assertions.reader_inference: The text does not give the grid resolution, the value of s, the genetic algorithm settings or the number of levels used for the benchmark graphs.

assertions.value: The authors state that each refinement phase linearly interpolates the coarser solution to the finer graph, reduces the QAOA parameter-grid size to the parameters of the top s solutions from the previous level, and uses those s candidates with the interpolated best solution as the initial population of the genetic algorithm.
quotes: Each subsequent refinement phase (Algorithm 1) begins by linearly interpolating the coarsest-level solution to the finer graph
we reduce the QAOA parameter-grid size to include only the parameters corresponding to the top s solutions from the previous level
These s candidates, along with the interpolation of the best solution from the coarsest level, are then used as the initial population of the genetic algorithm.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors describe their own refinement procedure in Section IV-B.
assertions.reader_inference: The pruning scheme is where the parameter transfer is used. The text refers to Section IV-B for the transfer rules, and the rules are in the text of that section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the refinement procedure adds minimal overhead (no optimization cost), because only the top solution from each level needs to be updated and quantum measurements or correlation-matrix computations are performed sparingly due to the parameter transfer, and that the same principle could be applied to sampled measurement outcomes in an experimental implementation.
quotes: the refinement procedure adds minimal overhead (no optimization cost)
quantum measurements or correlation-matrix computations are performed sparingly due to the parameter transfer
the same principle could be applied directly to the sampled measurement outcomes in experimental implementation
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about cost and a proposed extension, with no timing breakdown of the overhead in the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper simulates the correlation matrices classically at order n squared cost, so the claim of minimal overhead is about quantum resource use, not the measured run time of the simulation.

assertions.value: The authors define a heuristic similarity measure between the p = 1 QAOA landscapes of two hierarchy levels: they detect the grid points for which the average energy exceeds 3 standard deviations, and take the size of the intersection of the detected zones normalized by the size of their union.
quotes: We start by analyzing the effectiveness of the parameter transfer between levels for p = 1 QAOA landscape.
we detect all the grid points for which ⟨H⟩(γ,β) > 3σ(γ,β)
calculate the size (i.e., the number of grid points) of their intersection, normalized by the size of their union, which we treat as a heuristic similarity measure between two landscapes
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the measure in Section V-A.
assertions.reader_inference: The measure compares the location of high-deviation zones only. It does not compare the value of the optimal parameters between levels.

assertions.value: The authors report that for most hierarchy levels the p = 1 QAOA energy landscapes show a high degree of similarity (about 95% or more), with one anomalous point of about 75% similarity at the coarsest level, which they state is still a fairly high level of similarity.
quotes: We start by analyzing the effectiveness of the parameter transfer between levels for p = 1 QAOA landscape.
We observe that for most hierarchy levels, the QAOA energy landscapes exhibit a high degree of similarity (≳ 95%).
anomalous point with ∼ 75% similarity corresponds to the coarsest level
Despite being smaller than for the rest of the levels, it still constitutes a fairly high level of similarity
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result shown for one example graph (Fig. 3, levels 0 to 12).
assertions.reader_inference: The text does not name the graph of Fig. 3. The coarsest level, where the parameters are optimized and then transferred, is the level with the lowest similarity.

assertions.value: The authors state that, when performing the parameter transfer and pruning scheme, the optimized parameters at the coarsest level are expected to perform well in further levels.
quotes: when performing the parameter transfer and pruning scheme, the optimized parameters at the coarsest level are expected to perform well in further levels
assertions.certainty_reason: An expectation drawn by the authors from the landscape-similarity measure.
assertions.reader_inference: Overlap of high-deviation zones does not imply that the same parameters are optimal at each level, so this is an inference from a heuristic measure.

assertions.value: The authors report, on the G1 graph, that interpolating between levels using only QRR samples (scenario (1)) does not improve the coarsest solution and performs generally worse than a genetic algorithm initialized with QRR at the coarsest level (scenario (2)), and that the combination of both (scenario (3)) yields the best results.
quotes: we first set up the following experiments with the G1 graph
using only QRR samples to interpolate between levels (scenario (1)) does not improve the coarsest solution
performs generally worse than using the genetic algorithm initialized with QRR at the coarsest level (scenario (2))
the combination of both approaches (scenario (3)) yields the best results
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one graph in one study, simulated classically.
assertions.reader_inference: A single graph and, as far as the text shows, one run per variant. The text gives no repeat runs or spread.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the considered system sizes, the solutions from the multilevel QAOA p = 1 solver are not of sufficient quality to compete with state-of-the-art classical solvers.
quotes: the solutions obtained from the multilevel QAOA p = 1 solver are not of sufficient quality to compete with state-of-the-art (SoTA) classical solvers
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this limit of their solver at the opening of Section V.
assertions.reader_inference: This limits the abstract's wording of a high-quality solver and the closing line that results highlight the usefulness of the method.

assertions.value: The authors report that using the multilevel solver's solutions as a warm start for Burer-Monteiro provides an advantage in the majority of the tested cases with reduced total runtime, and that the warm-started run can give solutions better than the raw Burer-Monteiro implementation, which runs at least 800s longer in practice.
assertions.anchor: Section V and Section V-B, Table I, p.4-6
quotes: can lead to solutions better than the raw Burer-Monteiro implementation with the same or higher runtime (at least 800s higher in practice)

We observe that the initialization of the Burer-Monteiro algorithm via solutions obtained from the multilevel solver provides an advantage in the majority of the tested cases, while having reduced total runtime.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, simulated classically.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage is for the multilevel solution used as a warm start for a classical solver. It does not show that the p = 1 QAOA part adds value over the classical multilevel solver, apart from the roughly-half comparison in the stored assertion.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benchmark uses the Gset dataset with graph sizes from 5000 nodes up to 10000 nodes and graphs from the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection going up to 14000 nodes, that the genetic algorithm is implemented with PyGAD, and that the warm-started Burer-Monteiro is run for 100 seconds.
assertions.anchor: Section V and Section V-B, p.4-5
quotes: We look at the Gset dataset [41] with graph sizes from 5000 nodes up to 10000 nodes, and graphs from the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection [42] going up to 14000 nodes.
The genetic algorithm is implemented using PyGAD [43].
the warm-started Burer-Monteiro is run for 100 seconds
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the experimental setup in Sections V and V-B.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I lists a graph named facebook with 3437 nodes, below the 5000-node lower bound stated in the text. The table values are not quoted here.

assertions.value: The authors state that Table I compares their method with classical approaches, records the best objective, and names the classical global solvers BURER02, FES02GVP, DUARTE05 and GLOVER10, which the caption calls much slower than multilevel.
quotes: HERE, WE COMPARE OUR METHOD WITH WELL-KNOWN CLASSICAL APPROACHES, AND THE BEST OBJECTIVE IS RECORDED.
THE CORRESPONDING REFERENCES FOR (MUCH SLOWER THAN MULTILEVEL) CLASSICAL GLOBAL SOLVERS ARE BURER02 [40], FES02GVP [44], DUARTE05 [45], AND GLOVER10 [46].
assertions.certainty_reason: The caption states what the table compares.
assertions.reader_inference: The table has 17 graphs. Table numbers are not entered here because the text layer holds them as separate lines.

assertions.value: The authors state that their experimental instances have both positive and negative edge weights, which is beyond the traditional MAXCUT formulation, and that they use QUBO and MAXCUT interchangeably.
quotes: we will mention QUBO and MAXCUT interchangeably
Our experimental instances are both positive and negative weighted on wij which is beyond the traditional MAXCUT formulation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state this scope in footnote 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that their current implementation uses QRR to generate bitstring candidates because they can only simulate local expected values at large scale.
quotes: While our current implementation uses QRR to generate bitstring candidates (since we can only simulate local expected values at large scale)
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their implementation in Section IV-B.
assertions.reader_inference: No sampled measurement outcomes are used. The sampling variance of a real device is outside the reported results.

assertions.value: The authors state that numerical evidence suggests finer-level information is carried through coarsened levels and can be employed to forward subsequent refinements, reducing the search space and accelerating convergence.
quotes: Numerical evidence suggests that finer-level information is carried through coarsened levels and can be employed to forward subsequent refinements, reducing the search space and accelerating convergence.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion. The word suggests marks it as not proved.
assertions.reader_inference: The text has no figure of convergence speed against a baseline without transfer. Fig. 4 is described as approximation ratio and runtime per level for G1.

assertions.value: The authors state that classical simulation of the QAOA expectation values can be demanding for large-scale graphs, that the costs could potentially be reduced with quantum computers, and that quantum computers would also facilitate more performant optimization with higher-depth QAOA circuits.
quotes: hence it can be quite demanding for large-scale graphs
Those costs could potentially be reduced with the use of quantum computers.
they would also facilitate more performant optimization with higher-depth QAOA circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: An author expectation with no test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that source code and results are available at a link that will be provided upon acceptance, so this version of the paper gives no link.
quotes: Our source code and results are available at [link will be provided upon acceptance].
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement about the paper's own artifacts, with no link to check in this version.
assertions.reader_inference: No code or data could be checked from this version of the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing references [2] to [4], that large-scale implementation of QAOA remains impractical due to hardware constraints such as limited connectivity, short coherence times and high error rates, which restrict the size and depth of circuits that can be reliably executed.
quotes: large-scale implementation of QAOA remains impractical [2], [3] due to hardware constraints such as limited connectivity, short coherence times, and high error rates
which significantly restrict the size and depth of circuits that can be reliably executed [4]
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing references [31] to [33], that finding the optimal parameters of a parameterized quantum circuit is a hard task and in some cases NP-hard, and that variational quantum algorithm landscapes often exhibit barren plateaus when the circuit depth is large for big-scale problems, which might also apply to QAOA.
quotes: finding the optimal parameters to minimize a given observable is a hard task and, in some cases, NP-hard [31]
often exhibits barren plateaus when the circuit depth is large for big-scale problems [32], which might also apply to QAOA [33]
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: The text says barren plateaus might also apply to QAOA, which is a hedge, not a settled result.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing earlier work, that in parameter transfer methods the potentially suboptimal performance is traded for avoidance of the costly optimization steps by using a fixed set of parameters for multiple problem instances, irrespective of problem type.
quotes: In parameter transfer methods, the potentially suboptimal performance is traded for avoidance of the costly optimization steps through the use of a fixed set of parameters for multiple problem instances
assertions.certainty_reason: A description the paper attributes to other work.
assertions.reader_inference: This paper transfers parameters between levels of one instance's hierarchy, which differs from the fixed parameters across instances in the cited methods.
